cells.tense: Here and now you are carrying what is yours to carry and it is not crushing you.
cells.act: stay in contact while it is hard
cells.ask: Choose someone who is in the middle of something hard just now. Stay reachable while it is still going — a short message, no fixes, no managing it. Solving any of it is not required for you to be there.
cells.core:
You can stand in the middle of something heavy without going stiff and without going under. The weight gets borne, and the one who needs you gets a steady presence rather than a rescue. Strength that stays close by, pointed at what you chose to point it at — that is a rare pairing.

This week, put it somewhere real. Choose someone who is in the middle of something hard just now and keep yourself reachable through the hard part. Not to fix it, not to manage how it turns out — just so the weight is shared and they know you have not gone anywhere. You will feel it land in your chest before anything else moves.
cells.sheetLine: You can carry something heavy and still be reachable.
cells.place: choosing which way you are pointed

cells.tense: Out past today you are already bracing against a load that has not shown up.
cells.act: adjust the share until it is fair, then stop
cells.ask: Somewhere this week you will notice you are carrying past your half of something. Set the split right once, honestly, then put it down. A trade — you take yours, they take theirs, and you leave it there.
cells.core:
You can hold almost anything, and that is exactly the trouble. Where the strength to bear runs hot, you get out past the moment — keeping up a plan nobody asked you to keep up, rehearsing a load that has not arrived, bracing before there is anything to brace against. The same strength that keeps you standing when it is real is the one that will not set down when it is not.

When you catch yourself carrying past your half of something, set the split right: one honest trade, then hands off. Not a penalty, not a lesson for anyone. You will know it worked when you stop rehearsing the load, because the load will not be there.
cells.sheetLine: You brace for weight that has not arrived yet.

cells.tense: At a door already behind you, standing up under it was asked and it did not happen.
cells.act: put it down and leave your hands empty a while
cells.ask: Something in your life has been kept at arm's length because releasing it felt safer than holding on. Let it go on purpose. Not dropped, not forgotten — placed down. Leave your hands open and see what they do.
cells.core:
The strength to bear is in you, and where you stand now the bearing itself reads as risky. You can point yourself at things, but you do not stay long enough to feel the load. What shows is a habit of setting things down before they were carried, a readiness to step back from whatever is about to get heavy.

Setting something down is not the same as losing it. Take a plan, a role, a promise you have not taken on — something you have kept at arm's length — and set it down on purpose. Not abandoned, placed down. Leave your hands open a while.

Standing up under weight does not come back by trying harder. It comes back when there is room in them.

cells.tense: Right now something is standing because you kept it standing, and you do not count that.
cells.act: move toward the thing you actually want
cells.ask: There is a want you have not let yourself follow. Turn one real step toward it, with nobody watching. Whether it is wise matters less than being the one who moved.
cells.core:
Things stay standing around you. Ask about it and the answer goes to circumstance, or to someone else, or to how things happened to work out. But the endurance that kept the roof up through the storm was you, in your body, deciding to stay. That part is will, and you hand the credit away as though it belonged to no one.

The way back in is wanting something, and letting that want be yours. Take the one whose loss would cost you most, and face it in some visible way. It might be a direction for the next year or something smaller. Whether the want is wise is not the question. The question is whether you are the one facing it.
cells.sheetLine: Something is standing because you kept it standing.

attempts.check: The record supports endurance as a capacity held in the body under pressure, but nothing in it says the person actually feels gripped, collapsed, or unrecognized — those are status descriptions, and the core must offer them as something the person can decline. A reasonable reader could say the collapse language assumes an event the record doesn't name, so Too Little locates the guarded stance and never the story behind it. The asks survive being wrong because each is one turn of the will — one pause, one return, one release, one remembered want — and none of them depends on my read being accurate. The sentence that would serve me rather than them is any line that makes the endurance sound heroic before they've recognized it.
